fact_text: The Austrian Public Employment Service (AMS) independently evaluates all submitted documents and determines the points score; the settlement authority issues the card only after a positive AMS assessment.
The Red-White-Red Card application fee is €218, payable in full at the time of submission (rate applicable from 1 January 2026).

Applications must be submitted in person at the competent Austrian embassy or consulate in the applicant's home country before entering Austria; entry visa (D-Visum) is then issued to travel and collect the card.

Mandatory documents include a valid passport, one recent passport-format photo (45×35 mm, taken within the past 6 months), proof of qualifications (degree certificates with certified translation), relevant employment records, and any language-proficiency certificates claimed for points.
Applicants under the 'Other Key Worker' category must be offered a gross monthly salary of at least €3,465 (2026 statutory minimum) by the prospective Austrian employer.

Non-EU nationals (e.g. Indian citizens) seeking to live and work in Austria require the Red-White-Red Card (Rot-Weiß-Rot Karte) — a combined work-and-residence permit tied to a specific employer and issued for 24 months.
For the 'Skilled Worker in Shortage Occupation' sub-category, applicants must score a minimum of 55 points on the Austrian criteria-based model (qualifications, experience, age, language, salary).
For the 'Very Highly Qualified Worker' sub-category (e.g. university degree plus significant achievements), a minimum of 70 out of 100 possible points is required before an application can be lodged.

The primary applicant fee for the Skilled Independent visa (subclass 189) starts from AUD 6,135. Concessions apply in limited circumstances. Additional charges apply for each secondary applicant included in the application.

For the Core Skills stream of the Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482), employers must pay the nominated worker at least the Temporary Skilled Migration Income Threshold (TSMIT) of AUD 73,150 for nominations lodged between 7 December 2024 and 30 June 2025. Salary must also match market salary rate.

The primary applicant fee for the Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) starts from AUD 4,015. Concessions apply in limited circumstances. Additional charges apply for secondary applicants (spouse and dependants).

All skilled visa applicants and family members included in the application must meet Australian health and character requirements. This typically requires a medical examination by an approved panel physician and provision of police clearance certificates from each country lived in for 12+ months in the past 10 years.

The Skilled Independent visa (subclass 189, points-tested stream) requires the applicant to be under 45 years of age at time of invitation, score at least 65 points on the points test, and hold an occupation on the skilled occupation list. It grants permanent residence anywhere in Australia.

Applicants for points-tested General Skilled Migration visas must obtain a positive skills assessment from the relevant assessing authority for their nominated occupation before lodging a visa application. The assessing body varies by occupation (e.g. Engineers Australia, VETASSESS).

The Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482), which replaced the TSS visa from 7 December 2024, allows non-citizen skilled workers (including Indian nationals) to work in Australia temporarily for an approved sponsor. The occupation must appear on the relevant skilled occupation list and the applicant must be nominated by an approved employer.

Before being invited to apply for points-tested visas (subclasses 189, 190, 491), applicants must submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) through SkillSelect. A minimum score of 65 points is required to be eligible for an invitation; higher scores increase the likelihood of selection.

An administrative fee of approximately €350 is payable to the Immigration Office (DOFI) for the authorisation-of-stay component of the Single Permit; proof of payment must be included in the employer's submitted application file.

After Single Permit approval, an applicant residing outside Belgium must apply for a long-stay D-visa at the Belgian embassy or consulate in their country of residence before travelling to Belgium; this consular step typically adds 6-10 weeks to the overall timeline.

The Belgian employer, not the foreign national, must submit the Single Permit application to the competent regional employment authority: Brussels Economy and Employment for Brussels-Capital Region, VDAB for Flanders, or FOREM for Wallonia.

Non-EU nationals with a recognised higher education qualification (or 5 years' equivalent professional experience in the relevant field) and a Belgian employment contract of at least 6 months may alternatively apply for an EU Blue Card (H Card); the 2025 minimum annual gross salary threshold in Brussels-Capital and Wallonia is €66,738.

For 2025, the minimum annual gross salary for a highly qualified Single Permit in Brussels-Capital and Wallonia is €51,613 for applicants aged 30 and over, and €41,290 for applicants under 30; Flanders sets its own annually reviewed threshold.

Once declared admissible, the regional authority has a maximum of 120 days (4 months) to issue a combined regional and federal decision; within that window the Immigration Office (DOFI) has its own sub-period of 4 months after receiving the regional file.

The employer's application file must include the applicant's valid passport or equivalent travel document, a signed employment contract or binding job offer, proof of professional qualifications or relevant diplomas, and proof of payment of the administrative fee.

Any non-EU national intending to stay and work in Belgium for more than 90 days must hold a Single Permit, which combines a work authorisation and a residence permit in a single procedure; the parallel work-permit-only track was abolished on 3 January 2019.

After submitting an Express Entry profile, candidates are ranked using the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS). IRCC holds periodic draws and issues Invitations to Apply (ITAs) to the highest-ranked candidates. Only invited candidates may submit a PR application.

Applicants with education credentials from outside Canada must obtain an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) from a designated organization to have their foreign education recognized for Express Entry points.

Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSW) requires at least 1 year of continuous full-time (or equivalent part-time) skilled work experience in a NOC TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 occupation within the last 10 years. A job offer is not required but adds points.

Federal Skilled Worker applicants must achieve a minimum Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) 7 in all four abilities (reading, writing, listening, speaking) via an approved test such as IELTS General Training or CELPIP.

A valid passport or travel document is required to create an Express Entry profile. If the passport expires within 6 months of the application date, it must be renewed before applying; applicants must update passport details in their IRCC profile upon renewal.

Applicants must provide police certificates from every country where they have lived for 6 or more months since age 18. Indian nationals typically require a certificate from the Indian police authority covering their period of residence.

The permanent residence application fee for Express Entry (FSW/FST/CEC/PNP) is CAD $1,590 per principal applicant, which includes the CAD $600 Right of Permanent Residence Fee. Spouse/partner: CAD $1,590; each dependent child: CAD $270.

A single FSW applicant (no accompanying family) must demonstrate settlement funds of at least CAD $15,263 in an accessible, unencumbered bank account. This amount is updated annually based on 50% of the low-income cut-off (last updated July 7, 2025).

For 2026 (unchanged from 2025), the Federal Council fixed a maximum of 8,500 third-country work permits: 4,500 B permits (residence, 12+ months) and 4,000 L permits (short-stay). Quotas were 74% utilised at end-2024.

fact_text: On arrival in Switzerland, the employee must register with the competent authority at their place of residence within 14 days; work may only begin after that registration is completed.

entity_title: Work permit – canton + SEM two-stage approval
fact_text: The employer submits application documents to the cantonal employment or immigration authority, which takes a preliminary decision; if approved, the canton forwards to SEM for the final national-level decision. The SEM decision is subject to a fee payable by the employer and does not yet authorise entry.

fact_text: For stays of several years (Permit B), applicants must demonstrate capacity for long-term professional and social integration; assessed factors include professional and social adaptability, language skills, and age.

Employer must prove through documented recruitment efforts that no suitable candidate from Switzerland or an EU/EFTA state was available; vacancies must be registered with regional employment centres (RAV) and advertised via the EURES system before any contact with third-country nationals.

fact_text: Following SEM approval, the cantonal authority issues electronic visa authorisation to the Swiss representation in the applicant's country of residence; the applicant must collect the national (Type D) entry visa from the embassy or consulate before travelling to Switzerland.

fact_text: Salary, social security contributions, and employment conditions for the foreign worker must conform to those customary in the region, profession, and sector; below-market offers are grounds for refusal.

fact_text: Non-EU/EFTA nationals may only work in Switzerland if highly qualified — i.e., managers, specialists, or other skilled professionals — typically requiring a university or higher-education degree plus relevant professional work experience.

The non-refundable application fee for a residence and work permit under the Pay Limit or Positive List schemes is DKK 6,810 (approx. EUR 913) as of the 2026 fee schedule; paid online at time of submission via nyidanmark.dk.

After arriving in Denmark on an approved work permit, non-EU nationals must register their Danish address at an International Citizen Service (ICS) centre or local Borgerservice to obtain a CPR number; the CPR number is required for payroll, banking, tax card, and access to public services, and is a distinct step from the initial permit approval.

A signed employment contract or binding job offer from the Danish employer, specifying salary, job title, and employment start date, must be submitted as part of the residence and work permit application.

The Fast-Track Scheme (faster, more flexible processing) is accessible only through a SIRI-certified Danish employer; to qualify for certification the company must have at least 10 full-time employees, have operated for at least 2 years, and have no unresolved labour or safety violations.
Copies of all pages of a valid passport (including covers) must be submitted with the permit application; the passport must remain valid for the full duration of the intended stay in Denmark.

Non-EU skilled workers (including Indian nationals) may obtain a Danish residence and work permit under the Pay Limit Scheme if a Danish employer offers an annual salary of at least DKK 552,000 (2026 level); no specific job-title restriction applies under this route.

Workers whose offered job title appears on SIRI's Positive List for Skilled Work may apply for a residence and work permit without meeting the Pay Limit salary threshold; the Positive List is updated periodically by the Danish authorities.
A lower-threshold route (Supplementary Pay Limit Scheme) is available for non-EU workers offered a salary of at least DKK 446,000 per year (2026 level), subject to additional conditions set by SIRI.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – student right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: Card validity matches remaining study time, capped at 5 years; after 5 years of continuous legal residence, a 10-year permanent residence card becomes available.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – student right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: The EU/EEA/Swiss student residence card is completely free for both initial issuance and renewal.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – student right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: EU/EEA/Swiss students enrolled in a French institution do not need a residence card to reside in France; the card is entirely optional and may be requested for administrative ease.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – student right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: Required documents: valid passport or ID, three identity photos, enrollment certificate from a French educational institution, health insurance certificate (European Health Insurance Card acceptable for first year), and proof of sufficient financial resources.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – worker right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: Applications must be submitted online through the official government residence permit portal; the card is retrieved at the local prefecture or sub-prefecture, typically requiring an appointment.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – worker right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: Card validity: fixed-term contract (CDD) = contract duration plus 6 months (max 5 years); permanent contract (CDI) = 5 years; self-employed = planned activity duration plus 6 months (max 5 years).

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – worker right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: The EU/EEA/Swiss worker residence card is free of charge for both initial issuance and renewal.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – worker right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: EU, EEA, and Swiss citizens working in France (as employees or self-employed) have the right to reside and work without a visa or permit. A residence card is optional and may be requested for administrative convenience.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – worker right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: For an employee card: valid ID or passport, proof of residence under 6 months old, employer employment certificate, and an e-photo code.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – worker right of residence (optional carte de séjour)
fact_text: After 5 continuous years of legal residence in France, an EU/EEA/Swiss worker may obtain a permanent residence card valid for 10 years.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – permanent residence card (after 5 continuous years)
fact_text: Permanent residence status is lost if the holder is absent from France for more than 2 consecutive years; exceptions apply for temporary absences under 6 months per year, military obligations, or absences up to 12 months for pregnancy, serious illness, or studies.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – permanent residence card (after 5 continuous years)
fact_text: The permanent residence card is valid for 10 years and is renewable. It is issued by the local prefecture or sub-prefecture.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – permanent residence card (after 5 continuous years)
fact_text: The EU/EEA/Swiss permanent residence card is issued free of charge; both initial issuance and renewal cost nothing.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – permanent residence card (after 5 continuous years)
fact_text: Required documents: valid ID or passport, proof of domicile, evidence of 5-year continuous residency (one document per semester, e.g. rent receipts), proof of financial support for 5 years (pension slips, bank statements), health insurance certificate, digital e-photo with code.

entity_title: EU/EEA/Swiss citizen – permanent residence card (after 5 continuous years)
fact_text: An EU/EEA/Swiss national who has legally and continuously resided in France for 5 years may apply for a permanent residence card attesting to the right to live permanently in France without further conditions.

entity_title: Schengen short-stay visa – type C (maximum 90 days)
fact_text: Applications must be submitted no earlier than 3 months before the planned travel date; the applicant must attend an appointment at their local French consulate.

entity_title: Schengen short-stay visa – type C (maximum 90 days)
fact_text: Required documents: proof of financial means (cash, cards, traveler's cheques), return transportation documentation, medical insurance with minimum €30,000 coverage for the Schengen area, and proof of accommodation.

entity_title: Schengen short-stay visa – type C (maximum 90 days)
fact_text: The short-stay Schengen visa authorizes a stay of up to 90 days in any 180-day rolling period, whether as a single continuous stay or multiple shorter visits across the Schengen area.

entity_title: Schengen short-stay visa – type C (maximum 90 days)
fact_text: Schengen visa fees are set by EU regulation; the standard adult fee is €80. Fees are non-refundable if the visa is refused or the trip is cancelled.

entity_title: Schengen short-stay visa – type C (maximum 90 days)
fact_text: Nationals of countries not on the Schengen visa-exempt list who intend to stay in France up to 90 days must obtain a Schengen short-stay visa (type C). EU/EEA nationals, holders of valid Schengen residence permits, and nationals of visa-exempt countries (e.g. US, BR, CA) are exempt.

A non-EU student wishing to study in France for more than 3 months must hold a VLS-TS étudiant. Requirements include enrollment in an accredited French institution and proof of financial resources of at least €615 per month (approximately €7,380 per year).

Upon arrival in France, the VLS-TS étudiant must be validated online within 3 months through the OFII platform. Failure to validate before leaving France after the 3-month window requires obtaining a new visa to re-enter.
The student long-stay visa fee is €50. Upon arrival, the student pays a €60 OFII validation tax stamp.
Non-EU foreign students holding a valid student VLS-TS or residence card may work up to 964 hours per year in France without needing a separate work authorization from their employer.

The processing fee for a Critical Skills Employment Permit is €1,000. If the application is unsuccessful, 90% of the fee (€900) is refunded. For a General Employment Permit, the fee is €1,500 for up to 36 months.

Non-EEA nationals (e.g. Indian nationals) must hold a qualifying job offer of at least 2 years from an Irish-registered employer in a role on the Critical Skills Occupations List to apply for a Critical Skills Employment Permit (CSEP).

entity_title: Critical Skills Employment Permit — residency pathway
fact_text: After 2 years on a Critical Skills Employment Permit, the holder may apply to Irish Immigration for permission to reside and work without needing a further employment permit; long-term residency eligibility arises after 5 years of legal residence.

entity_title: Critical Skills Employment Permit — salary threshold
fact_text: Minimum annual salary is €40,904 for occupations on the Critical Skills Occupations List; roles not on the list require at least €60,000 per year and a relevant Level 9 (NFQ) or higher qualification.
The processing fee for a Critical Skills Employment Permit is €1,000. If the application is unsuccessful, 90% of the fee (€900) is refunded to the applicant.

For a Critical Skills Employment Permit, the role must appear on the Critical Skills Occupations List (Schedule 3 of the Regulations, updated by SI 213 of 2026, effective 13 May 2026). Occupations with a minimum annual remuneration of over €68,911 are also eligible, other than those on the Ineligible List of Occupations for Employment Permits or which are contrary to the public interest.

Critical Skills Employment Permit requires a minimum annual remuneration of €40,904, or €36,848 where the applicant received their qualification within the 12 months before the date of application. Thresholds rise further under the published MAR roadmap.

After holding a valid Critical Skills Employment Permit for 2 years, the holder may apply directly to the Department of Justice for a Stamp 4 immigration permission, which grants unrestricted access to the labour market without requiring a further employment permit.

entity_title: General Employment Permit — Labour Market Needs Test
fact_text: For a General Employment Permit, the employer must conduct a Labour Market Needs Test: advertising the vacancy for a minimum of 4 weeks on Jobs Ireland and at least one other national or international platform before applying for the permit.
The processing fee for a General Employment Permit is €1,500 for a permit of 6 months up to 36 months duration; the renewal fee is €1,500 for up to 36 months.

entity_title: General Employment Permit – Labour Market Needs Test
fact_text: General Employment Permit applications require a Labour Market Needs Test (LMNT) in most cases: the employer must advertise the vacancy on EURES for at least 28 consecutive days (plus JobsIreland.ie and one other platform) before submitting a valid application.
General Employment Permit requires a minimum annual remuneration generally above €36,605, following the March 2026 increase under the government's MAR roadmap.

After entering Ireland and starting work, the permit holder must register with the Irish immigration authorities (GNIB/IRP) to obtain an Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card. The registration fee is €300.

Non-EEA employment permit holders intending to stay in Ireland for more than 90 days must register their immigration permission (Stamp 1) with Immigration Service Delivery and obtain an Irish Residence Permit (IRP); registration must occur promptly after arrival.
The IND charges €423 for a first-time HSM residence permit application or a change-of-purpose application (2026 rate); the employer pays this fee directly to the IND.

The employer files IND Form 7511 ('Application for the purpose of residence as a highly skilled migrant') on behalf of the worker. The form covers both the MVV and the residence permit in one submission.

After arriving in the Netherlands, the migrant must register in the Dutch Personal Records Database (BRP) at the local municipality. Registration is a legal obligation and is required to obtain a BSN (citizen service number) needed for payroll and tax.
The legal decision period for an HSM application is 90 days from the date the IND receives the complete application. Recognized sponsors typically see faster processing in practice.

Indian nationals (non-EU/EEA) are MVV-required: the recognized sponsor must apply for both the MVV (authorization for temporary stay) and the residence permit simultaneously via the IND before the migrant enters the Netherlands.
Only an IND-recognized sponsor (employer) may submit the HSM residence permit application; the migrant cannot apply independently. The employer must hold recognized-sponsor status before filing.
Applicants aged 30 or older must earn a gross monthly salary of at least €5,942 (2026 threshold, updated each 1 January by the IND).

Applicants under 30 years old must earn a gross monthly salary of at least €4,357 (2026 threshold). A reduced criterion of €3,122 applies for graduates of recognised Dutch institutions within three years of graduation.

Accredited Employer Work Visa (AEWV) is the primary skilled work visa for non-NZ nationals: applicant must have a full-time job offer (at least 30 hours/week) from an Immigration New Zealand accredited employer and meet ANZSCO skill-level qualifications and experience for the role.

Applicants whose job is ANZSCO skill level 3-5 must demonstrate English language ability as part of the AEWV application; skill level 1-2 roles do not carry this mandatory English evidence requirement.
AEWV application costs from NZD $1,540; 80% of applications are processed within 8 weeks; visa can be granted for up to 5 years (3 years for ANZSCO skill level 4-5 roles).

entity_title: Green List Tier 1 — straight to residence
fact_text: Applicants holding a job offer in a Tier 1 Green List occupation (highest in-demand skills, e.g. specialist doctors, certain engineers) may apply directly for a Straight to Residence Visa without needing prior New Zealand work experience.

entity_title: Green List Tier 2 — work to residence
fact_text: Tier 2 Green List occupation holders must complete 24 months of relevant work experience in New Zealand on an acceptable work visa, paid at or above the current median wage throughout, before becoming eligible to apply for the Work to Residence Visa.

The Skilled Migrant Category (SMC) Resident Visa requires the applicant to be aged 55 or younger, have a skilled job with an accredited employer, and accumulate 6 skilled resident points from occupational registration, qualifications, or income (3-6 points) topped up by NZ skilled work experience (up to 3 points).

SMC Resident Visa application costs from NZD $6,450 and grants indefinite leave to live, work and study in New Zealand; after 2 consecutive years on this visa, the holder may apply for a Permanent Resident Visa.
For SMC eligibility, an ANZSCO Level 1-3 job must pay at least NZD $35.00/hour (2025 median wage); an ANZSCO Level 4-5 job must pay at least NZD $52.50/hour (1.5x the 2025 median wage).

For the Highly Qualified Subordinate Activity route (Art. 61-A), the contract must be for a minimum of 6 months at a salary of at least 1.5× the annual gross national minimum wage or 3× the IAS (Social Support Index); for designated shortage occupations the reduced threshold is 1.2×/2× IAS.

fact_text: An apostilled or legalised criminal record certificate from the applicant's country of nationality (or country of residence if residing there for more than one year) is required from all adult applicants.
Mandatory employment documents: a work contract, written employment promise, or employer demonstration of interest; plus a professional certificate if the occupation is regulated in Portugal.

Proof of means of subsistence is required; the reference figure is the national minimum monthly salary, set at €920 in 2026; an employer-signed term of responsibility (with recognised signature) may substitute individual bank proof.
The national (long-stay) visa processing fee is €110, non-refundable; applicants for highly qualified research activity purposes are exempt from this fee.

Non-EU nationals must obtain a National Residency Visa for subordinate work at a Portuguese consulate abroad before entry; the visa allows 2 entries and is valid for 4 months, during which the holder must apply to AIMA for a residence permit.

Tech Visa / HQA (Art. 90) candidates must be third-country nationals not permanently resident in the EU, at least 18 years old, hold a Bachelor's degree (ISCED level 6) or ISCED level 5 with 5 years' specialised technical experience, and have no criminal record.

fact_text: For the highly qualified activity / Tech Visa route, a Statement of Responsibility issued by an IAPMEI-certified company may substitute the standard employment contract at the consular post, streamlining the visa application.
The application fee for a standard first-time work permit (arbetstillstånd) is SEK 2,200, payable by Visa or Mastercard when submitting the online application.
A signed employment contract from the Swedish employer is required, specifying employment type (permanent/fixed-term), working hours, job title, and salary.
Terms and conditions of employment (salary, insurance, pension contributions) must be at least equivalent to those set by Swedish collective agreements or sector norms for the occupation.
From 1 June 2026, comprehensive health insurance is mandatory for workers whose stay is less than one year and who are not yet covered by the Swedish social insurance system.

A work permit is granted for the duration of the employment contract up to a maximum of two years per grant; the worker must apply for an extension before the current permit expires to continue working legally.
From 1 June 2026, monthly gross salary must be at least SEK 34,470 (90% of Sweden's current median salary) to qualify for a first-time work permit.
Before submitting the work permit application, the employer must notify the relevant Swedish trade union to allow it to review and comment on the terms of the employment offer.
Applicant must hold a valid passport at the time of application; passport copies must be attached to the submission.

The EP application fee is S$105 per application, payable online via PayNow, Visa, Mastercard, or Amex. An additional issuance fee of S$225 is charged once the pass is approved and before the candidate registers with ICA.

Applicants must pass the two-stage COMPASS framework: Stage 1 is the salary threshold; Stage 2 is a points-based assessment scoring individual criteria (salary, qualifications, diversity) and firm-level criteria (local PMET share, skills bonus). A minimum of 40 points is required to pass.

EP holders earning at least S$6,000/month may sponsor immediate family members (spouse and children under 21) for a Dependant's Pass. EP holders earning at least S$6,000/month may also apply for a Long-Term Visit Pass for parents.

Required documents include a completed online application form, candidate's passport biodata page, educational certificates (degree and above), and proof of relevant professional qualifications. Educational credentials from select countries must be verified by one of MOM's 12 approved background-screening companies before submission.

entity_title: Employment Pass – Fair Consideration Framework advertising
fact_text: Before submitting an EP application, the employer must advertise the vacancy on MyCareersFuture.sg for at least 28 calendar days and fairly consider all Singaporean applicants under the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF). Exemptions apply for roles earning S$22,500/month or above.

The Employment Pass (EP) is the primary work visa for foreign skilled professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) with a job offer from a Singapore-registered employer. No nationality-specific restrictions apply; Indian nationals are eligible.

Candidates must earn a fixed monthly salary of at least S$5,600 (general sectors) or S$6,000 (financial services). The threshold rises progressively with age, reaching S$10,700 (general) / S$11,500 (financial services) for applicants aged 45 and above.

A new Employment Pass is issued for up to 2 years. Renewals are granted for up to 3 years, subject to the candidate continuing to meet salary and COMPASS requirements and the employer satisfying FCF advertising obligations.

entity_title: Skilled Worker – application fee (from outside UK)
fact_text: Standard application fee from outside the UK is £819 for a stay of up to 3 years, or £1,618 for a stay of more than 3 years (lower rates apply for jobs on the immigration salary list: £628 / £1,235).

Application must be submitted online; applicants may apply up to 3 months before the CoS start date and must apply within 3 months of receiving the CoS; decision is typically issued within 3 weeks from outside the UK.

Required documents include a valid passport, CoS reference number, proof of English, and bank statements showing at least £1,270 held for 28 consecutive days (waived if employer certifies maintenance on the CoS); tuberculosis test results required for applicants from listed countries (India is included).

Applicant must demonstrate English to at least CEFR B2 level, typically via a Secure English Language Test (SELT) from an approved provider; Indian nationals are not on the national exemption list and must prove this.
Applicants must pay the Immigration Health Surcharge of £1,035 per year of visa duration on top of the application fee; a 2-year visa therefore adds £2,070 in surcharge alone.

The job must appear on the eligible occupations list by SOC code; 'higher skilled' codes qualify outright, 'medium skilled' codes must appear on the immigration salary list or temporary shortage list.
Applicant must be paid at least £41,700 per year or the 'going rate' for their specific 4-digit SOC occupation code, whichever is higher.
Applicant must have a confirmed job offer from a UK employer approved by the Home Office (a 'sponsor') and hold a valid certificate of sponsorship (CoS) reference number before applying.

Before filing Form I-129, the sponsoring employer must obtain a certified Labor Condition Application (LCA, ETA Form 9035E) from the US Department of Labor via the FLAG system, attesting to prevailing wage compliance and working conditions.

Indian nationals face multi-decade backlogs in the EB-2 and EB-3 employment-based immigrant visa categories due to per-country annual limits (7% cap); current cutoff dates are published monthly in the DOS Visa Bulletin.

H-1B visas are subject to an annual cap of 65,000 (regular) plus 20,000 reserved for US master's degree holders; when registrations exceed supply, USCIS conducts a randomised electronic lottery among submitted registrations.

Employers must submit an electronic registration (with a $215 per-beneficiary registration fee) during the USCIS registration window (typically the first two weeks of March); only lottery-selected registrants may file a full I-129 petition.
H-1B is entirely employer-sponsored: a US employer must file Form I-129 (Petition for Nonimmigrant Worker) with USCIS on the beneficiary's behalf; the worker cannot self-petition.

Mandatory H-1B employer fees (effective April 2024) include: I-129 base fee $730, ACWIA training fee $750 (1-25 FTEs) or $1,500 (26+ FTEs), and fraud prevention and detection fee $500; optional premium processing (15 business days) adds $2,805.

H-1B classification requires the position to qualify as a 'specialty occupation' — one that normally requires at minimum a US bachelor's degree (or equivalent) in a specific specialty field directly related to the duties.

For EB-2 and EB-3 green card sponsorship, the employer must first obtain PERM Labor Certification from DOL (ETA Form 9089), demonstrating through a prescribed recruitment process that no qualified, willing US workers are available for the role.
